newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Montenegro Bar port handles 1.3 mln T in 9 months.
newsitem.headline: Montenegro Bar port handles 1.3 mln T in 9 months.

text.p: Yugoslavia's biggest port, Luka Bar, handled 1.3 million tonnes of cargo in the nine months since sanctions against rump Yugoslavia were suspended last November, the Belgrade daily Nasa Borba reported on Monday.

"We are working at 25-30 percent capacities because the Yugoslav economy cannot begin operating at full steam until the external wall of sanctions is lifted," the daily quoted Luka Bar general manager Petrasin Kasalica as saying.
"We invoiced around 50 million dinars in the nine month period," a source in the company's financial department told Reuters.

The port depended on business mostly from large metal complexes in Serbia like Sartid 1913 of Smederevo, RTB Bor and Trepca of Kosovska Mitrovica, and Montenegro's aluminium plant of Podgorica, the Niksic steel works and Jugopetrol of Kotor.

"The port can easily handle five million tonnes of cargo, but we have to wait until large systems in Serbia, such as the Zastava (automobile) Group, the Nis and Kraljevo (engineering) regions, Rakovica (motors) and other firms of the metal complex are reactivated," Kasalica said.
He said dumping prices offered by ports in Bulgaria and Greece were damaging the port's business as well as late payments from Yugoslav customers.
Luka Bar, which employs a total of 1,760 workers, is one of Montenegro's biggest public enterprises.
The total value of the port has been estimated at around 800-900 million German marks, of which 70 percent is state property which cannot be sold, he said.
Kasalica said the remaining 30 percent, worth around 250 million marks, is to be privatised.
"Of this, 40 percent has already been distributed to workers (30 percent free and 10 percent at a discount), and the remainder to three state funds."
The three state funds have been set up by Montenegro's Agency for Privatisation as an intermendiate stage in the privatisation process.
Kasalica said his goal was to bring in foreign capital that would be invested in facilities for offshore business.
"My basic idea is that the port should be even freer than a free trade zone. We have great space for foreign capital, all the conditions for offshore operations and for concessions."
